body: None of the early signals in these cases was secret. Each was **public data that sat inside a boring or declining story**: segment revenue (NVIDIA), mix shift (Radico), a new CEO's product reset (Royal Enfield), a policy document (defence, PLI) or an import-substitution capex (Deepak). The skill lies in following the chain of consequences to the point the market has not yet priced. Steinhardt formalised this as **"variant perception"**: a well-founded view meaningfully different from consensus. Every idea had to state the consensus view, the variant view and a trigger event, and he held positions until the disagreement closed ([MicroCapClub](https://microcapclub.com/michael-steinhardt-in-his-own-words/)). Marks's example captures the second-order step. First-level thinking says "earnings will fall; sell." Second-level thinking says "earnings will fall less than people expect; the surprise lifts the stock; buy" ([Oaktree](https://www.advisorperspectives.com/commentaries/2015/09/24/it-s-not-easy)). Soros's reflexivity adds the dynamic element. Rising prices bring capital, flows and analyst upgrades that reinforce the narrative, until the gap with reality breaks. **Booms are long and busts are short and sharp** ([GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/421890/george-soros-theory-of-reflexivity)). That pattern fits India's PSU, defence and railway run of 2023–24.
